passage:
Ward note, 7 p.m. — Jagdish, staff nurse, children's ward
Ishu, 5, needed his drip line changed. His mother, Preeti, stood close, stroking his hair and saying, "Oh no, baby, it's going to hurt, I'm so sorry," in a shaking voice. Ishu screamed before I had touched his arm. I asked Preeti to sit at the head of the bed and tell him about his new school bag. I spoke slowly: "Ishu, you'll feel a small pinch, then it's done. Squeeze Mummy's finger." He cried, but less, and stopped soon after. Preeti looked stunned. Later she told me she hadn't realised how much of her fear was passing to him. I showed her how to hold his hand steadily. Reminder for the team: our tone is part of the treatment.

qa.q: What did Jagdish ask Preeti to talk about?
qa.a: Ishu's new school bag.

qa.q: What did Preeti realise afterwards?
qa.a: She hadn't realised how much of her own fear was passing to Ishu; her shaking voice had made him expect pain and scream before he was touched.

qa.q: Which choices helped Ishu through the drip change?
qa.a: Jagdish spoke slowly and honestly about a small pinch, gave Ishu Mummy's finger to squeeze, and moved Preeti to the head of the bed with a calm topic.

qa.q: What is the drip change like for Ishu when his mother is frightened?
qa.a: For Ishu, his mother's fear is a signal that something terrible is coming, so he screams before anything happens; once the voices are calm, the same pinch is easier to bear. 🤍

grounding: A nurse notices that a mother's anxious hovering makes her child's pain worse while a calm, confident voice settles him.

passage:
Sunday night
Lulu fell off the swing today and cut her knee. I ran to her first, and my voice went high: "Oh God, blood, are you okay, are you okay?" She looked at my face and howled. I kept patting everywhere, checking her arms, her head. She cried harder. Then Thomas knelt down, calm as anything. "Hey, brave girl. Let's look together. It's a scratch. We'll wash it and put a dinosaur plaster on." Lulu sniffed, stared at her knee and asked for the green dinosaur. That was it. I've been thinking about it all evening. The cut was the same. My panic made it bigger for her; his steadiness made it smaller. Next time, deep breath first.
Noor

qa.q: What kind of plaster did Lulu ask for?
qa.a: The green dinosaur one.

qa.q: What does Lulu howling at Noor's face suggest about what she was feeling?
qa.a: She seemed to read the panic on Noor's face as a sign that something was badly wrong, so her fear grew far beyond the small cut.

qa.q: What is Noor's plan for next time, and why could it help?
qa.a: Taking a deep breath first, so Noor's voice stays steady; like Thomas's calm, it would tell Lulu the hurt is manageable.

qa.q: If you were Lulu, how would the two grown-ups feel different?
qa.a: One is frightened and patting everywhere, which makes the cut seem scary; the other kneels calmly and calls it a scratch, which makes it feel small and safe.

grounding: A young parent notices that their own panicked hovering made a child's small cut feel worse, while Thomas's calm, confident voice settled her.

passage: Payal, twenty-four, was in her second month as a trainee nurse at the primary health centre outside Sagar. That afternoon a farmer carried in his son, Chotu, six, with a thorn deep in his heel. The father kept wiping the boy's face and saying, 'Arre, arre, it's going to hurt so much, my poor boy.' Chotu screamed each time anyone came near. Then Vandana Didi, the senior nurse, pulled up a stool. She spoke low and slow. 'Chotu, look at this window. Count the parrots on that tree. I'm going to clean your foot. One small pinch, then done.' Chotu sniffed and started counting. Vandana asked the father to hold his hand and help count. The thorn came out on 'four'. Chotu cried for a moment, then stopped. Payal watched the father's shoulders drop. She wrote in her notebook: the voice is part of the dressing.

qa.q: What did Vandana Didi ask Chotu to count?
qa.a: She asked him to count the parrots on that tree.

qa.q: What did Payal realise from watching Vandana Didi?
qa.a: Payal realised that the calm, slow voice was part of the care, since Chotu settled and the thorn came out with little fuss.

qa.q: How did Vandana Didi involve the father, and why was that wise?
qa.a: She asked him to hold Chotu's hand and help count, which turned his worry into calm support instead of anxious hovering.

qa.q: What was the visit like for Chotu's father?
qa.a: At first he was frightened and kept telling his son it would hurt, but his shoulders dropped once he had a helpful job and saw his son calm.

passage: Saturday football practice in Lisbon was nearly over when seven-year-old Gabriel went down clutching his ankle. Nadia, twenty-five and the team's volunteer coach, jogged over, but Gabriel's mother got there first. 'Oh no, oh no, is it broken? Gabi, does it hurt a lot? Where? Here? Here?' With every question, Gabriel sobbed harder. Nadia knelt beside them. She kept her voice slow and even. 'Hi, Gabi. You took a big tumble. Let's see together. Can you wiggle your toes for me?' He wiggled them, hiccuping. 'Good. We'll put the ice pack on, and you can tell me which player you were chasing.' His mother, watching, took a breath and started stroking his hair instead of pressing his foot. Gabriel's crying slowed to sniffs. Nadia said, 'If it's still sore tomorrow or it worries you, have a doctor look.' His mother nodded, calmer too.

qa.q: What did Nadia ask Gabriel to do first?
qa.a: She asked him to wiggle his toes.

qa.q: How did Gabriel's mother seem to feel when she reached him first?
qa.a: She was very frightened, asking whether it was broken and where it hurt, over and over.

qa.q: What did Nadia do that changed the moment, and what did she still advise?
qa.a: She spoke slowly, checked his toes, gave him an ice pack and something to talk about, and still said a doctor should look if it was sore tomorrow or worrying.

qa.q: How might Gabriel's mother see the moment afterwards?
qa.a: She may notice that her own worried questions made Gabriel cry harder, and that his crying slowed once she matched Nadia's calm.

grounding: A young football coach sees that her calm, steady voice settles a hurt child while his mother's anxious questions were making it worse.

passage:
In the paediatric ward at nine at night, Shreya, a nurse on her first year, watched her colleague Parveen try to calm a boy with a cut hand. Parveen was kind, but kept saying, "Oh no, oh no, does it hurt a lot? Tell me if it hurts!" The boy's crying got louder with every question.
Shreya stepped in to hold the dressing tray. She knelt and spoke slowly. "Hi. I'm Shreya. We're going to clean this and it'll sting for a moment. Then you can choose a sticker. Ready?"
The boy hiccupped, watched her face, and held still. The sting came; he winced but didn't scream.
Afterwards, Parveen said quietly, "I was scaring him, wasn't I?" Shreya shook her head. "You care a lot. It just shows in your voice."

qa.q: What could the boy choose after the dressing?
qa.a: He could choose a sticker.

qa.q: What was Shreya feeling as Parveen kept asking if it hurt?
qa.a: Shreya felt concerned, noticing that the boy's crying got louder with each anxious question.

qa.q: What could any caregiver learn from what Shreya did?
qa.a: A slow, confident voice, a clear warning about the sting and a small choice can settle a frightened child during care.

qa.q: How might Parveen feel after asking "I was scaring him, wasn't I?"
qa.a: Parveen may feel embarrassed but grateful, since Shreya answered kindly and helped explain what happened.

grounding: A nurse sees that a calm, confident voice settles a child in pain while a colleague's anxious questions made it worse.

passage:
Dear Ankita Didi,
Remember how nervous I was about Kabeer's vaccination? Something happened today I want to tell you.
Last time, I held him, kept saying "sorry, sorry, baby, it's okay, sorry," and my voice shook. He screamed before the needle even touched him.
Today I watched the nurse instead. She didn't hover. She smiled at him, said to me, "Mummy, just hold him steady. Quick pinch, then the bird on the wall," and pointed at a painted bird. I copied her. I held him steady and talked about the bird, calm, like it was ordinary.
He cried for maybe five seconds and then went back to looking at the bird.
I think he was listening to my voice more than feeling the needle. My worry was part of what hurt him last time.
Love,
Gargi

qa.q: What did the nurse point at on the wall?
qa.a: She pointed at a painted bird.

qa.q: What was Gargi feeling when noticing the difference between the two visits?
qa.a: Gargi felt relieved and a little regretful, realising that her shaky, worried voice last time had added to Kabeer's distress.

qa.q: What could Gargi keep doing at future visits?
qa.a: She could stay steady, speak calmly and give Kabeer something to look at, like the nurse did, instead of anxiously apologising.

qa.q: How might Kabeer have experienced the two visits differently?
qa.a: At the first visit Kabeer probably picked up his mother's fear and screamed early; at the second, her calm voice made the pinch feel smaller.

grounding: A young mother notices that a calm, confident voice settles her baby during a jab, while her anxious hovering had made it worse.

passage:
Pradeep, you asked what the hardest part of being a children's nurse is. Honestly? It's the parents. I'm Nitin, three years on the ward, and I love them, but listen.
Last week a girl came in with a broken wrist. Her father kept pacing, saying, "Is she okay? Is it bad? Be careful, be careful!" Every time he said it, her face crumpled and she screamed louder.
So I sat down at her level and said, in my most boring voice, "This bit will hurt for a moment. Then we put on a cast, and you choose the colour." She watched me. She breathed. She picked purple.
Then I asked her father to hold her other hand and just breathe with her. He did, and she calmed down even more. How you say it matters as much as what you do. That's what I've learned.

qa.q: What colour cast did the girl pick?
qa.a: She picked purple.

qa.q: What was Nitin feeling as the girl's father paced?
qa.a: Nitin felt concerned, noticing that each anxious "be careful" made the girl's face crumple and her screams louder.

qa.q: Which step did Nitin take to include the father helpfully?
qa.a: Nitin asked the father to hold her other hand and just breathe with her, giving his care a calm shape.

qa.q: How might the girl have felt when Nitin spoke in a boring voice?
qa.a: She probably felt steadier and less frightened, because the calm voice suggested nothing terrible was happening.

grounding: A nurse notices a calm, steady voice settles a hurt child while a parent's anxious hovering makes it worse.

I'm Madhav, a trainee nurse, and on Tuesday I watched the same child twice in one hour. The first time, the boy's father was holding his hand while his grazed knee was cleaned. The father kept saying, "Oh no, oh no, is it hurting? Beta, is it very bad?" His voice shook. The boy screamed louder with every question.
Then Amandeep, the senior nurse, came for the second dressing. She knelt at his level and said slowly, "This will sting for a moment, then it gets better. Squeeze my finger and count the fish on the wall with me." The boy was still crying a little, but softer, and he counted to six. The father watched her too.
I can't say what the boy felt inside, but his face changed.

qa.a: The fish on the wall.

qa.a: Madhav seemed struck and curious, noticing how differently the same child reacted to an anxious voice and a calm one.

qa.q: What could the father try at the next dressing?

qa.q: How might the father have felt watching Amandeep?

passage:
Chinmay, sit a minute. You're rushing around that little girl like the building's on fire. Let old Maria tell you something. When I was twenty-four, new on the children's ward in Kochi, a boy came in with a broken arm. His mother was frantic, touching his face, crying, "My baby, my poor baby." He screamed until the windows shook.
Then Sister Thresiamma walked in. She didn't rush. She pulled up a stool, sat at his eye level and said, "I know it hurts a lot. We're going to help it. Tell me the name of your cat." He stopped mid-scream to say, "Pinky." I watched his breathing slow while she talked.
Same arm, same pain, different voice. I never forgot it. Now go back slowly, and lower your voice.

qa.a: Maria was likely struck and relieved, amazed that a calm voice could slow the boy's breathing with the same pain.

qa.a: She sat at his eye level, spoke calmly, admitted the pain and gave him something else to think about.

qa.a: She may have felt relieved and perhaps realised her frantic crying had added to his fear.

It was a crowded Saturday night in the hospital's children's ward, and the lights kept flickering. Hemant, a trainee nurse, watched two things happen at once.
In bed 3, a boy with a cut hand was screaming. His aunt hovered over him, saying, "Oh god, oh god, is it deep? Will it scar?" The more she panicked, the louder he cried.
Then Vidya, the senior nurse, came over. She knelt, smiled and said in a slow voice, "I'm going to clean this. It will sting for a moment, then it'll feel better. You can squeeze my hand."
The boy's cries slowed. His aunt went quiet too.
Hemant wrote in his notebook: Calm words are medicine too.

passage:
At the park near her flat in Gangtok, Pema watched her neighbour Thomas's little daughter fall off the swing and scrape her knee.
The girl's grandmother rushed in first, wringing her hands. "Hai, blood! She's hurt, she's hurt!" The girl screamed louder.
Thomas walked over, crouched and said calmly, "I see it. A scrape. Let's wash it and put a plaster. You were so brave on that swing."
The girl looked at her knee, then at her father's calm face. Her crying slowed to hiccups.
Pema noticed how the same scrape looked completely different depending on who was talking. That evening, when her nephew bumped his head, she remembered and spoke slowly.

qa.a: She fell off the swing.

qa.q: What did Pema notice, and how did she feel about it?
qa.a: She noticed the calm voice settled the child while panic worsened it, and she felt struck enough to try it herself.

qa.q: What helped the girl calm down?
qa.a: He stayed calm, named the injury simply, told her the plan and praised her, which helped her settle.

qa.q: How did the grandmother's panic affect the girl?
qa.a: It frightened the girl more, making her scream louder.

grounding: Shows a neighbour observing that a parent's calm, confident voice settles a hurt child while anxious hovering makes it worse.

passage: I'm Sunaina, a junior nurse on the children's ward, and last week I learned something no textbook said clearly. A little boy came in with a cut on his arm that needed cleaning. His mother was frantic, hovering, saying, "Oh no, oh no, it's going to hurt so much." He screamed before anyone touched him. Then Lakshmi, our senior nurse, knelt down. Her voice was slow and warm. "I'm going to clean this. It'll sting a little, and then it's done. Can you count the fish on my badge?" He counted. He winced, but he didn't scream. His mother watched, and her shoulders dropped. I realised the way Lakshmi spoke wasn't extra to the care. It was part of the care.

qa.a: Sunaina felt surprised and impressed, realising that a calm voice is part of the care itself, not an extra.

qa.q: What could Sunaina copy from Lakshmi when caring for a scared child?
